verses.zh: 你以为有理，或以为你的公义胜于　神的公义，
verses.en: “Do you think this to be[NOTE:1] justwhen[NOTE:2] you say, ‘My right before God’?[NOTE:3]
notes: This short speech falls into two sections: Elihu refutes Job’s claim that goodness avails nothing (35:2-8), asserting that when the cry of the afflicted goes unanswered they have not learned their lesson (35:9-16).
The line could be read as “do you reckon this for justice? Here “to be” is understood.
The word “when” is not in the Hebrew text, but is implied.

verses.zh: 才说这与我有甚么益处？我不犯罪比犯罪有甚么好处呢？
verses.en: But you say, ‘What will it profit you,’[NOTE:1] and, ‘What do I gain by not sinning?’[NOTE:2]
notes: The brief line could be interpreted in a number of ways. The MT simply has “my right from God.” It could be “I am right before God,” “I am more just/right than God” (identifying the preposition as a comparative min (מִן); cf. J. E. Hartley, Job [NICOT], 463), “I will be right before God,” or “My just cause against God.”
The referent of “you” is usually understood to be God.

verses.zh: 我要回答你和在你这里的朋友。
verses.en: I[NOTE:1] will reply to you,[NOTE:2] and to your friends with you.
notes: The Hebrew text merely says, “What do I gain from my sin?” But Job has claimed that he has not sinned, and so this has to be elliptical: “more than if I had sinned” (H. H. Rowley, Job [NCBC], 224). It could also be, “What do I gain without sin?”
The emphatic pronoun calls attention to Elihu who will answer these questions.

verses.zh: 你要向天观看，瞻望那高于你的穹苍。
verses.en: Gaze at the heavens and see;consider the clouds, which are higher than you.[NOTE:1]
notes: The Hebrew text adds, “with words,” but since this is obvious, for stylistic reasons it has not been included in the translation.

verses.zh: 你若犯罪，能使　神受何害呢？你的过犯加增，能使　神受何损呢？
verses.en: If you sin, how does it affect God?[NOTE:1] If your transgressions are many,what does it do to him?[NOTE:2]
notes: The preposition is taken here as a comparative min (מִן). The line could also read “that are high above you.” This idea has appeared in the speech of Eliphaz (22:12), Zophar (11:7-8), and even Job (9:8-11).
Heb “him” (also in v. 7); the referent (God) has been specified in the translation for clarity.

verses.zh: 你若是公义，还能加增他甚么呢？他从你手里还接受甚么呢？
verses.en: If you are righteous, what do you give to God,or what does he receive from your hand?

verses.zh: 你的过恶或能害你这类的人；你的公义或能叫世人得益处。
verses.en: Your wickedness affects only[NOTE:1] a person like yourself,and your righteousness only other people.[NOTE:2]
notes: See Job 7:20.

According to Strahan, “Elihu exalts God’s greatness at the cost of His grace, His transcendence at the expense of His immanence. He sets up a material instead of a spiritual stand of profit and loss. He does not realize that God does gain what He desires most by the goodness of men, and loses what He most loves by their evil.”tn The phrase “affects only” is supplied in the translation of this nominal sentence.

verses.zh: 人因多受欺压就哀求，因受能者的辖制（原文是膀臂）便求救，
verses.en: “People[NOTE:1] cry out because of the excess of oppression;[NOTE:2] they cry out for helpbecause of the power[NOTE:3] of the mighty.[NOTE:4]
notes: Heb “and to [or for] a son of man, your righteousness.”
The word “people” is supplied because the sentence only has the masculine plural verb.
The final noun is an abstract plural, “oppression.” There is no reason to change it to “oppressors” to fit the early versions. The expression is literally “multitude of oppression.”
Heb “the arm,” a metaphor for strength or power.

verses.zh: 却无人说：造我的　神在哪里？他使人夜间歌唱，
verses.en: But no one says, ‘Where is God, my Creator,who gives songs in the night,[NOTE:1]
notes: Or “of the many” (see HALOT 1172 s.v. I רַב 6.a).

verses.zh: 教训我们胜于地上的走兽，使我们有聪明胜于空中的飞鸟。
verses.en: who teaches us[NOTE:1] more than[NOTE:2] the wild animals of the earth,and makes us wiser than the birds of the sky?’
notes: There have been several attempts to emend the line, none of which are particularly helpful or interesting. H. H. Rowley (Job [NCBC], 225) says, “It is a pity to rob Elihu of a poetic line when he creates one.”
The form in the text, the Piel participle from אָלַף (ʾalaf, “teach”) is written in a contracted form; the full form is מְאַלְּפֵנוּ (meʾallefenu).

verses.zh: 他们在那里，因恶人的骄傲呼求，却无人答应。
verses.en: Then[NOTE:1] they cry out—but he does not answer—because of the arrogance of the wicked.
notes: Some would render this “teaches us by the beasts.” But Elihu is stressing the unique privilege humans have.

verses.zh: 虚妄的呼求，　神必不垂听；全能者也必不眷顾。
verses.en: Surely it is an empty cry[NOTE:1]—God does not hear it;the Almighty does not take notice of it.
notes: The adverb שָׁם (sham, “there”) connects this verse to v. 11. “There” can be locative or temporal—and here it is temporal (= “then”).

verses.zh: 何况你说，你不得见他；你的案件在他面前，你等候他吧。
verses.en: How much less, then,when you say that you do not perceive him,that the case is before him and you are waiting for him![NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “surely—vanity, he does not hear.” The cry is an empty cry, not a prayer to God. Dhorme translates it, “It is a pure waste of words.”

verses.zh: 但如今因他未曾发怒降罚，也不甚理会狂傲，
verses.en: And further,[NOTE:1] when you saythat his anger does not punish,[NOTE:2] and that he does not know transgression![NOTE:3]
notes: The point is that if God does not listen to those who do not turn to him, how much less likely is he to turn to one who complains against him.
The expression “and now” introduces a new complaint of Elihu—in addition to the preceding. Here the verb of v. 14, “you say,” is understood after the temporal ki (כִּי).
The verb פָּקַד (paqad) means “to visit” (also “to appoint; to muster; to number”). When God visits, it means that he intervenes in one’s life for blessing or cursing (punishing, destroying).

verses.zh: 所以约伯开口说虚妄的话，多发无知识的言语。
verses.en: So Job opens his mouth to no purpose;[NOTE:1] without knowledge he multiplies words.”
notes: The word פַּשׁ (pash) is a hapax legomenon. K&D 12:275 derived it from an Arabic word meaning “belch,” leading to the idea of “overflow.” BDB 832 s.v. defines it as “folly.” Several define it as “transgression” on the basis of the versions (Theodotion, Symmachus, Vulgate). The RSV took it as “greatly heed,” but that is not exactly “greatly know,” when the text beyond that requires “not know at all.” The NIV has “he does not take the least notice of wickedness.”
